chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad informed me, from his father, from Aḥmad ibn Idrīs and Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from Abī ʿAbd Allāh, from Ḥammād, from Muḥammad ibn al-Nuʿmān, from Ghālib ibn al-Hudhayl, who said:
I asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:
"And wipe your heads and your feet up to the ankles."

Is it in the genitive reading or in the accusative reading? He عليه السلام said: “Rather, it is in the genitive reading.” This drops the basis of the question. Then even if we were to concede that the recitation with the genitive is equal to the recitation with the accusative—since among the seven reciters Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, and in the narration of Abī Bakr from ʿĀṣim recited it with the genitive, while Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī, and in the narration of Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim recited it with the accusative—it would still also require wiping, because the grammatical position of the heads is one of accusative due to the governing verb, which is wiping, falling upon it, and the heads were only put into the genitive by the letter bāʾ. On this basis, it is not objectionable that the feet be coordinated to the grammatical position of the heads, not to their wording, and thus be accusative while the obligation concerning them is wiping, just as it is for the heads. Coordination according to grammatical position is permissible and well known in the language of the Arabs. Do you not see that they say: “I am not standing, nor sitting,” so “sitting” is put in the accusative according to the position of “standing,” not its wording? Likewise they say: “I roughened his chest and Zayd’s chest,” and “Indeed Zayd is in the house, and ʿAmr,” so ʿAmr is raised according to position because inna and what it governs are in a nominative position. Similar to this in their speech is: “If you come to me, then you shall have a dirham, and I shall honor you”; since their saying “then you shall have a dirham” is in the position of jussive, “and I shall honor you” is coordinated to it and made jussive. Similar to it is: “Whomever Allah leads astray, there is no guide for him, and He leaves them...” with jussive according to the position of the word “guide,” because it is in a jussive position. The poet said: “Muʿāwiyah, indeed we are human, so be gentle; we are not mountains, nor iron.” So “iron” was put in the accusative according to the position of “mountains.” Another said: “Will you send a dīnār for our need, or ʿAbd Rabb, brother of ʿAwn ibn Mikhraq?” He only put ʿAbd Rabb in the accusative because the proper construction of the speech would be “sending a dīnār,” so he carried it according to the position, not the wording. They have even permitted what is more remote than this, because they coordinated according to meaning even if the wording does not require it, as in the poet’s saying: “Bring me the like of Banī Badr for their people, or the like of the family of Manẓūr ibn Sayyār.” Since the meaning of “bring me” is “give me” or “present to me,” he said “or the like of” in the accusative, coordinating according to the meaning. If it is said: What do you deny in saying that the recitation with the accusative requires only washing and does not admit wiping, because coordinating the feet to the position of the heads in establishing obligation is an expansion and figurative usage, while the apparent sense and literal reality require coordinating them to the wording, not the position? We say: The matter is not as you have imagined. Rather, coordination according to grammatical position is approved in the language of the Arabs and permissible, not merely by way of expansion and departure from literal usage. The speaker has a choice between carrying the inflection according to the wording at one time and according to the position at another. This is manifest in Arabic and well known among its people, and in the Qur’an and poetry it has many parallels. Moreover, even if we were to concede that coordination to the wording is stronger, then coordinating the feet to the position of the heads would still be preferable with the accusative recitation, because the accusative of the feet can only be on one of two bases: either by coordination to the hands and faces in washing, or by coordination to the position of the heads, so that they are accusative while their ruling is wiping. Coordinating them to the position of the heads is more appropriate, because when a statement contains two governing factors, one near and the other far, applying the nearer one is preferable to applying the farther one. The grammarians have explicitly stated this. They said: if one says, “He honored me and I honored ʿAbd Allāh,” and “I honored and ʿAbd Allāh honored me,” then attaching the noun mentioned after the two verbs to the second verb is more appropriate than attaching it to the first, because the second is nearer to it. The Qur’an and most poetry have come with applying the second. Allah the Exalted said: “And that they thought as you thought that Allah would never raise anyone,” because had He applied the first, He would have said, “as you thought it.” And He said: “Bring it to me that I may pour over it molten brass”; had He applied the first, He would have said, “that I may pour it.” And He said: “Here, read my book”; had He applied the first, He would have said, “Here, read it, my book.” The poet said: “Every creditor exacted and fulfilled his claim, while ʿAzzah’s creditor remained delayed and troubled.” So he applied the second, not the first, because had he applied the first, he would have said, “fulfilled it, his creditor.” Among what the second was applied to is the poet’s saying: “And bay horses bloodied, as though along their backs there had run over them and clothed them with the color of gold.” Had he applied the first, he would have raised “color,” whereas in the narration it is accusative. Similar to it is the saying of al-Farazdaq: “But had I reviled Niṣf and Banū ʿAbd Shams of Manāf and Hāshim reviled me...” He said “Banū” because he applied the second, not the first. As for the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays, in which he applied the first: “If what I strive for were merely the lowest livelihood, a little wealth would have sufficed me, and I would not have sought...” then the first thing about it is that it is anomalous, outside its proper category, and no judgment is based on what is anomalous. Second, he only used the nominative because he did not make the little amount the object sought; rather, what he sought was kingship, and he made the little amount sufficient. Had he not intended this and put it in the accusative, the meaning would have been corrupted.

Al-Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, said: The two ankles are the two raised domes of the feet in front of the shanks, up to his statement: and it is that which rises from it in its middle, as we have mentioned. What indicates this is His Exalted saying, “up to the ankles,” for He clarified that the endpoint of wiping is up to the two ankles. Had He intended what our opponents hold, He would have said “up to the anklebones,” because in each foot there are two of those. Another indication is the consensus of the Ummah: the Ummah is between two positions—one position says wiping alone is obligatory and does not permit choice, and decisively holds that what is meant by the two ankles is what we have mentioned; and another says washing is obligatory, or washing and wiping by way of choice, and says that the two ankles are the two protruding bones behind the shank—and there is no third position. So when the proof we have already mentioned establishes the obligation of wiping the two feet and that nothing else is permissible, what we have said concerning the true nature of the two ankles is established. This also indicates that.

ai.seo_question: Does the Qur’an command wiping or washing the feet in wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This text discusses the Qur’anic phrase regarding wudu (ablution), arguing that the verse indicates wiping the feet rather than washing them. It supports this through a narration from Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام, variant Qur’anic recitations, Arabic grammatical analysis, and a discussion of the meaning of the two ankles.
